uncited: This method projects a 3D Gaussian primitive, defined by a mean and a covariance matrix in world space, onto the 2D image plane to create a screen-space Gaussian splat.
- 3D Gaussian parameters: mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^3$, rotation quaternion $q$, scale vector $s$, opacity $\alpha$, spherical harmonic coefficients $h$.
- Camera parameters: View matrix $V$, Projection matrix $P$, image dimensions $W \times H$, focal lengths $f_x, f_y$, principal point $c_x, c_y$.
- Projected 2D mean $\mu_{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ (pixel coordinates).
- Projected 2D covariance $\Sigma_{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$.
- Inverse 2D covariance (conic) $\Sigma_{2D}^{-1}$.
Convert the parameterized rotation $q$ and scale $s$ into a $3 \times 3$ covariance matrix $\Sigma$.
Transform the covariance from world space to camera (eye) space using the rotation block of the view matrix $V$.
Linearize the perspective projection at $\mu_c = (x_c, y_c, z_c)$.
The projection function maps 3D camera coordinates to 2D pixel coordinates.
Apply the Jacobian to the camera-space covariance to obtain the screen-space covariance.
Add a small constant $\epsilon_{2d}$ to the diagonal elements of $\Sigma_{2D}$ to ensure positive definiteness and prevent aliasing/undersampling.
Compute the inverse of the stabilized $2 \times 2$ matrix analytically.
Project the 3D mean to screen coordinates.
Calculate the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2}$ and eigenvectors $e_1, e_2$ of $\Sigma_{2D}$.
The bounding box is the axis-aligned box enclosing the parallelogram spanned by $b_1$ and $b_2$ centered at $\mu_{2D}$.
It computes semi-axes using the trace and determinant of the covariance matrix and derives rotation components using half-angle identities.
**Time Complexity:** $O(M)$ for projection of $M$ Gaussians, where each projection involves constant-time matrix operations.
Rasterization is $O(N \cdot K)$ where $N$ is pixels and $K$ is average splats per pixel.
**Memory Complexity:** $O(M)$ to store projected Gaussians.
The closed-form projection avoids ray marching, which is the bottleneck in neural radiance fields.
**Strengths:** Differentiable, fast, handles view-dependent color via SH, preserves Gaussian form locally.
Aliasing can occur if the low-pass filter is insufficient.
